subChunks.title: groupingBy, partitioningBy & Custom Collectors
subChunks.hookHtml: Sorting spells by school, splitting them by power tier, counting enchantments by type — the Collectors API turns raw streams into rich, structured data with a single terminal operation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
groupingBy

Collectors.groupingBy(classifier) collects stream elements into a Map<K, List<V>> grouped by the classifier function. Add a downstream collector to further process each group.

List<String> spells = List.of("Fireball", "Frost", "Fire Storm", "Thunder");

// Group by first character
Map<Character, List<String>> byLetter = spells.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.charAt(0)));
// {F=[Fireball, Frost, Fire Storm], T=[Thunder]}

// Group and count each group (downstream collector)
Map<Character, Long> countByLetter = spells.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        s -> s.charAt(0),
        Collectors.counting()  // downstream: count elements per group
    ));
// {F=3, T=1}

partitioningBy

Collectors.partitioningBy(predicate) is a specialised groupingBy that always produces exactly two keys: true and false. It's more expressive and slightly faster when you have a binary split.

Map<Boolean, List<String>> partition = spells.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(s -> s.length() > 5));

List<String> longSpells  = partition.get(true);  // ["Fireball", "Fire Storm", "Thunder"]
List<String> shortSpells = partition.get(false); // ["Frost"]

// With downstream counting
Map<Boolean, Long> counts = spells.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(s -> s.length() > 5, Collectors.counting()));
// {true=3, false=1}

Downstream Collectors

The second argument to groupingBy/partitioningBy is itself a Collector applied to each group. Common downstreams: counting(), summingInt(), averagingInt(), mapping(mapper, downstream), joining(delimiter), toUnmodifiableList().

// Sum spell lengths per starting letter
Map<Character, Integer> totalLength = spells.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        s -> s.charAt(0),
        Collectors.summingInt(String::length)
    ));

// Collect names as joined string per group
Map<Character, String> joinedNames = spells.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        s -> s.charAt(0),
        Collectors.mapping(String::toUpperCase, Collectors.joining(", "))
    ));

Collectors.teeing

Java 12+ Collectors.teeing(downstream1, downstream2, merger) applies two collectors simultaneously to the same stream and merges the results — like splitting the stream into two collectors without iterating twice.

// Count both long and short spells in one pass
var result = spells.stream().collect(
    Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.filtering(s -> s.length() > 5, Collectors.counting()),
        Collectors.filtering(s -> s.length() <= 5, Collectors.counting()),
        (longCount, shortCount) -> longCount + " long, " + shortCount + " short"
    )
);
System.out.println(result); // e.g. "3 long, 1 short"

toUnmodifiableList and Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap

Use these to collect results into immutable containers — prevents accidental mutation of collected data and signals intent clearly.

List<String> immutable = spells.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.startsWith("F"))
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());
// immutable.add("X"); // throws UnsupportedOperationException

storyBeats.text: The Academy's grand grimoire needed organising — hundreds of spells by school, power, and length. No mage wanted to write sorting loops by hand. The Collectors API was their salvation.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: groupingBy is your indexer. Hand it a classifier — the first letter, the school, the tier — and it returns a map with every element sorted into its rightful group.

storyBeats.speaker: groupingBy
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: partitioningBy is the binary blade — it cleaves your collection into exactly two halves: those that satisfy a predicate, and those that don't.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The real power emerges with downstream collectors — chain counting(), summingInt(), or joining() after groupingBy and you perform aggregation per group in a single expression.
The grimoire sorted itself in milliseconds. Fire spells here, Frost there, each group counted and catalogued — the entire arcane library organised with a single terminal operation.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Given List<String> spells = List.of("Fireball","Frost","Fire Storm","Thunder","Frost Nova","Flare"):

  1. Use groupingBy(s -> s.charAt(0)) to group spells by their first character. Print each entry in the format "F=[Fireball, Frost, Fire Storm, Flare]" by iterating the map's entrySet().
  2. Use partitioningBy(s -> s.length() > 5) to split into long and short spells. Print the count of long spells using partition.get(true).size() prefixed with "Long spells: ".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a 'downstream collector' is in groupingBy and give two examples of when you'd use one. What is the difference between groupingBy and partitioningBy, and when would you specifically reach for partitioningBy over groupingBy?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, given a list of spells ["Fireball","Frost","Fire Storm","Thunder","Frost Nova","Flare"], use groupingBy on the first character of each spell and print each entry. Also use partitioningBy to split spells longer than 5 characters from shorter ones, and print "Long spells: " followed by the count of long spells.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The second argument to groupingBy/partitioningBy — a collector applied within each group. Enables single-pass aggregation: count, sum, join, or map elements per group.
A downstream collector that applies a mapping function before passing elements to another downstream. Useful for transforming group elements before collecting them.
Java 12+ collector that processes the stream through two downstream collectors simultaneously and merges results with a BiFunction. Avoids iterating a stream twice.
Collects a stream of CharSequences into a single String, with optional delimiter, prefix, and suffix. Only works on String streams (use mapping() to convert first).
Returns a collector producing an immutable list (backed by List.of()). Use when the collected result should never be modified after collection.
Collects a stream into a Map using key and value extractor functions. Throws IllegalStateException on duplicate keys unless a merge function is provided.
A downstream collector that counts elements in a group. Equivalent to stream().count() but usable as a downstream to groupingBy.
The three type parameters: T = input element type, A = accumulator/mutable container type, R = final result type. Understanding this helps when writing custom Collectors with Collector.of().

questions.questionHtml: What type does Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.charAt(0)) return when used as a terminal collector on a Stream<String>?
questions.explanationHtml: The classifier s -> s.charAt(0) returns a Character, so the key type is Character. Without a downstream collector, the values are List<String> — all elements mapped to that key.

questions.questionHtml: What does this print? (Assume HashMap iteration order — focus on values, not key order.)
questions.explanationHtml: cat and car start with 'c' (true partition, count 2). bat and bar do not (false partition, count 2). partitioningBy with counting() downstream gives {true=2, false=2}.

questions.questionHtml: This code throws an exception at runtime. What is the problem?
questions.correctAnswer: Duplicate key 'Fireball' causes IllegalStateException — add a merge function: (a, b) -> a
questions.explanationHtml: Collectors.toMap() throws IllegalStateException when two elements produce the same key. Fix: provide a merge function as the third argument — e.g., (existing, newVal) -> existing to keep the first value.

options: When you have more than 2 possible groups
When you want Map<String, List<T>> instead of Map<Boolean, List<T>>
When the classifier is a boolean predicate and you want to guarantee both true and false keys are always present
When performance is critical — partitioningBy is always faster
questions.correctAnswer: When the classifier is a boolean predicate and you want to guarantee both true and false keys are always present
questions.explanationHtml: partitioningBy always produces both true and false keys, even if one group is empty. groupingBy on a boolean lambda will omit a key if no elements map to it — which can cause NPEs when you call map.get(false).

subChunks.title: flatMap, peek, and Stream of Streams
subChunks.hookHtml: A library of spellbooks, each containing multiple spells — to search them all at once, you must first unfold the books into a single flat scroll. That's exactly what flatMap does.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
flatMap — Flattening Nested Collections

flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>) maps each element to a stream and then flattens all those streams into one. Essential for working with nested collections or Optional chains.

List<List<String>> spellbooks = List.of(
    List.of("Fireball", "Frost"),
    List.of("Thunder", "Heal", "Shield"),
    List.of("Blizzard")
);

// Without flatMap: Stream<List<String>> — still nested
// With flatMap: Stream<String> — everything flattened
List<String> allSpells = spellbooks.stream()
    .flatMap(Collection::stream)  // each List becomes a stream
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 5)
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [Blizzard, Fireball, Shield, Thunder]

peek — Debug Side Effects

peek(Consumer) is an intermediate operation that passes each element through unchanged but lets you observe it — perfect for debugging pipelines without breaking them.

List<String> result = spells.stream()
    .peek(s -> System.out.println("Before filter: " + s))
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 5)
    .peek(s -> System.out.println("After filter: " + s))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// Never use peek for real business logic — it's purely diagnostic!

Primitive Streams: IntStream, DoubleStream, LongStream

Specialized streams avoid boxing overhead. mapToInt(), mapToDouble() convert an object stream to a primitive stream. These offer sum(), average(), min(), max(), summaryStatistics().

int totalLength = spells.stream()
    .mapToInt(String::length)
    .sum();

OptionalDouble avg = spells.stream()
    .mapToInt(String::length)
    .average();

IntStream.range and rangeClosed

Factory methods for generating ranges of integers — range(start, end) is exclusive of end; rangeClosed(start, end) is inclusive.

// Print squares 1..5
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
    .map(n -> n * n)
    .forEach(System.out::println); // 1, 4, 9, 16, 25

// Generate first 5 even numbers
IntStream.iterate(0, n -> n + 2)
    .limit(5)
    .forEach(System.out::println); // 0, 2, 4, 6, 8

Stream.iterate and Stream.generate

Stream.iterate(seed, f) produces an infinite stream: seed, f(seed), f(f(seed)), ... Always limit() or use the Java 9 predicate overload. Stream.generate(Supplier) produces an infinite stream of supplier calls — e.g. random numbers or UUIDs.

// Fibonacci (simplified)
Stream.iterate(new int[]{0, 1}, arr -> new int[]{arr[1], arr[0] + arr[1]})
    .limit(8)
    .mapToInt(arr -> arr[0])
    .forEach(System.out::println); // 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13

// Random spells
Stream.generate(() -> "Spell-" + (int)(Math.random() * 100))
    .limit(3)
    .forEach(System.out::println);

storyBeats.text: Three spellbooks arrived at the Academy — each sealed, each containing different enchantments. To search them all at once required a technique that could dissolve the book boundaries entirely.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: flatMap is the great unfolding. Each nested collection becomes its own stream, and then all those streams merge into one continuous river of elements. The outer structure dissolves.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: peek is my diagnostic lens — I slip it between operations to watch elements pass through without disturbing the flow. Never rely on it for real logic; use it only to illuminate what's happening.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: For numerical work, IntStream.rangeClosed gives you a precise range. Map it, filter it, sum it — all without boxing a single Integer object.
The three spellbooks dissolved into a single flat stream. Filtered, sorted, and printed in moments — the arcane search engine the Academy had long dreamed of.

Part 1: Given List<List<String>> spellbooks = List.of(List.of("Fireball","Frost"), List.of("Thunder","Heal","Shield"), List.of("Blizzard")), use flatMap to create a single stream of all spells, filter those with length() > 5, sort them, collect to a list, and print each spell.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what flatMap does differently from map when you have a list of lists. What would happen if you used map instead of flatMap with Collection::stream? Also explain why peek should never be used for business logic — what fundamental guarantee about streams makes it unreliable for that purpose?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, write a program with a List of Lists of spells (at least 3 books with varying spell names). Use flatMap to flatten them, filter spells with more than 5 characters, sort them, collect to a list, and print each. Then use IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5) to print the squares of 1 through 5.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: map(f) wraps each element: Stream<List<T>> → Stream<List<T>>. flatMap(f) unwraps and merges: Stream<List<T>> → Stream<T>. Use flatMap whenever the mapper returns a collection or stream.
Intermediate stream operations (filter, map, flatMap, peek) are lazy — they execute only when a terminal operation (collect, forEach, count) is called. This enables short-circuiting optimisations.
range(0, 5) produces 0,1,2,3,4 (end exclusive). rangeClosed(1, 5) produces 1,2,3,4,5 (end inclusive). The distinction matters in loop-like patterns.
Converts an IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream back to a Stream<T> using a mapping function. Useful when you need to return to object operations after numeric processing.
Concatenates two streams lazily. Alternative to flatMap when combining exactly two streams. Avoid creating deeply nested concat chains — they can cause StackOverflowError.
Creates an infinite stream from a Supplier. Always pair with limit() or takeWhile(). Useful for generating test data, random sequences, or constant streams.
Java 9+ methods. takeWhile(predicate) returns elements while predicate holds; stops at first failure. dropWhile(predicate) skips elements while predicate holds, then returns the rest.
Returned by IntStream.summaryStatistics(). Provides count, sum, min, max, and average in a single pass — more efficient than computing each separately.

questions.questionHtml: What is the return type of stream.flatMap(Collection::stream) when the stream contains List<String> elements?
questions.explanationHtml: flatMap maps each List<String> to a Stream<String> and then flattens all those streams into a single Stream<String>. This is the key difference from map, which would return Stream<Stream<String>>.
rangeClosed(1,4) = 1,2,3,4. filter(n % 2 == 0) keeps 2,4. map(n * 10) gives 20, 40. forEach prints each on its own line.

questions.questionHtml: This code should produce a flattened list of all spell names, but it produces a Stream<Stream<String>> instead. What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: Replace .map(Collection::stream) with .flatMap(Collection::stream) to flatten the nested streams
questions.explanationHtml: map(Collection::stream) converts each list to a stream but keeps the outer stream wrapping, yielding Stream<Stream<String>>. flatMap(Collection::stream) merges all inner streams into one Stream<String>.

questions.questionHtml: You want to debug a stream pipeline by printing each element between two filter operations. Which approach is correct?
options: Use forEach() between the filters — this is safe and idiomatic
Use peek() between the filters for diagnostic logging only, knowing it may not fire if the pipeline is short-circuited
Split the stream into two separate streams and collect between filters
Use map(e -> { System.out.println(e); return e; }) — this is the recommended approach
questions.correctAnswer: Use peek() between the filters for diagnostic logging only, knowing it may not fire if the pipeline is short-circuited
questions.explanationHtml: peek() is the intended diagnostic tool. However, it may not be called if the terminal operation short-circuits (e.g., findFirst()). Never put essential business logic in peek(). forEach() is a terminal operation and would break the chain.
